phonemes.desc: Aspirate [h] running straight into the trilled [r] — an initial cluster Old Norse kept but English dropped, as in hringr 'ring' versus its silent-h descendants.
Short close back rounded [u], the vowel of 'put', held brief between the r and the nasal.
Velar nasal [ŋ] plus a fully sounded stop [g] — Old Norse sounded both, as in English 'finger', never the bare nasal of 'singer'.
Second [n], short [i], and the final nominative -r, lightly trilled — the masculine agent ending that marks him as a doer.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HRUNG-nir' — begin with a breathy h, roll the r straight into a short 'oo' as in 'put', sound both the ng and the g as in 'finger', and trill the final r.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Hrungnir, the strongest of the jötnar; no secure cognate or agreed etymology survives in the handbooks.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᚼᚱᚢᚴᚾᛁᛦ (h-r-u-k-n-i-R), the Viking-Age carving of the name; ᚴ writes both k and g, and ᛦ the final nominative -r.

kin.label: Skaldic attestation
kin.form: Hrungnir, named and fought in Þjóðólfr of Hvin's Haustlöng (early 10th c.), the oldest sustained witness to the duel.

pronunciation.note: Hrungnir is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses. The name's obscurity is a statement about etymology, never about the giant: the handbooks register Hrungnir's origin as uncertain while his duel with Þórr is among the best-attested single combats in the corpus.

domains.title: Giant, Duel with Thor
domains.subtitle: The Stone Heart, the Golden Mane, and the Wager of a Head
domains.lead: Hrungnir is the strongest of the jötnar — the stone-hearted giant who rode his gold-maned stallion Gullfaxi into Ásgarðr on a wager of heads, drank Thor's liquor from the god's own horns, boasted he would carry off Valhǫll, and met Mjǫllnir at Grjótúnagarðar with nothing in his hand but a whetstone. His duel is the most fully narrated single combat between god and giant in the Old Norse corpus.

cards.name: Gullfaxi
cards.desc: 'Golden mane' — the stallion Óðinn envied aloud, whose speed Hrungnir wagered his head against Sleipnir to disprove.

cards.name: The Whetstone
cards.desc: His weapon of stone — hurled against Mjǫllnir, it shattered in mid-air; one shard fathered every whetstone rock on earth, one lodged in Thor's skull.

cards.name: The Stone Heart
cards.desc: Three-cornered, sharp-edged, and hard — the Edda says his heart, head, and shield were all of stone, a giant made of his own weapon's material.

cards.name: Grjótúnagarðar
cards.desc: The 'stone-fence-yard' at the edge of heaven and giantland, where the single combat was appointed — the oldest named duelling-ground in the myths.

symbols.name: The whetstone
symbols.meaning: The honing-stone hurled against the hammer — stone against iron, and the shard still buried in Thor's head

symbols.name: Gullfaxi
symbols.meaning: The gold-maned stallion whose speed was worth a giant's head — and ended in the hands of three-night-old Magni

symbols.name: The three-cornered stone heart
symbols.meaning: Courage of the wrong material: resolve that is hard, sharp, and entirely without flexibility

symbols.name: Mǫkkurkálfi
symbols.meaning: The nine-league clay giant with a mare's heart — the giants' engineered champion, terror to look at and nothing within

symbols.name: The fallen foot
symbols.meaning: Hrungnir's leg across Thor's neck, which all the Æsir together could not lift — the weight of the foe after the foe is dead

mythology.lead: Hrungnir has essentially one story, and it is the greatest fight in the Edda: the wager, the drunken boasting in the hall of the gods, the appointed duel at Grjótúnagarðar, the shattered whetstone, and the fall that left even victorious Thor pinned beneath his enemy's leg. Snorri tells it in Skáldskaparmál, and the skald Þjóðólfr of Hvin had carved it into verse three centuries earlier.

myths.title: The Wager of Heads
myths.text: It begins with a boast Óðinn could not keep to himself. Riding Sleipnir through Jötunheimr, he met the giant Hrungnir, who asked who this man was with the golden helmet, riding so well over sea and air, and praised the horse. Óðinn answered with the stake that decides everything after: he wagered his head that no horse in Jötunheimr was Sleipnir's equal. Hrungnir sprang to his own stallion Gullfaxi, the gold-maned, and gave chase in a fury. The race ran to the very gates of Ásgarðr — and Hrungnir, carried past his own turning, galloped through them and in among the gods.

myths.title: Drunk in the Hall of the Gods
myths.text: The Æsir received him with the hospitality due an uninvited guest: they set before him the great horns Thor himself drank from, and Hrungnir emptied them one after another. Drunk, he let the boasts out — he would take Valhǫll up and carry it off to Jötunheimr, he would sink Ásgarðr, he would kill all the gods, save only Freyja and Sif, whom he would carry home; and the mead, he said, he would drink up all by himself. The Æsir, tired of the noise, named Thor; and Thor came in swinging his hammer, demanding who had given jötnar leave to drink in Valhǫll. Hrungnir, looking at him with anything but friendly eyes, answered that Óðinn had invited him and he stood under Óðinn's protection — then claimed his rights: Thor would gain little honour from killing him unarmed. It would be a greater trial of courage, he said, if Thor dared meet him in single combat at the frontier, at Grjótúnagarðar. And Thor, Snorri says, would by no means refuse a challenge to single combat.

myths.title: Grjótúnagarðar: The Whetstone and the Hammer
myths.text:
The giants made much of the appointment, for Hrungnir was the strongest of them and they expected one outcome or the other to be decisive. For his second they built a champion of clay: Mǫkkurkálfi, nine leagues tall and three leagues broad across the chest, with no heart big enough for the frame — so they gave him a mare's heart, and it quaked within him when Thor came. Hrungnir stood with his heart of stone, three-cornered and sharp-edged, his head of stone, and his broad shield of stone, holding his hone — the whetstone — before him. Þjálfi ran ahead and called out that Thor was coming from below, and Hrungnir, fearing a strike through the earth, set the shield beneath his feet and stood on it.

Then Thor came in an ásmegin-fury, lightning running before him, and hurled Mjǫllnir from afar. Hrungnir threw the hone with both hands, and the weapons met in the air. The hone burst in two: one half fell to earth, and from it come all the whetstone rocks in the world; the other half drove into Thor's head, and he fell forward. But Mjǫllnir did not stop — it struck Hrungnir's head and crushed the skull to small pieces, and the giant fell forward across Thor, his foot lying on Thor's neck. Þjálfi went at Mǫkkurkálfi, and the clay giant fell with little glory.

myths.title: The Foot No God Could Lift
myths.text: Then the strangest aftermath in the corpus: Thor lay pinned, and neither he nor Þjálfi could shift the giant's foot from his neck. All the Æsir came, when they learned, and together they could not lift it. At last came Magni, son of Thor and the giantess Járnsaxa — three nights old — and threw Hrungnir's foot off his father, saying it was a pity he had come so late: he thought he would have struck the giant dead with his fist. Thor gave him Gullfaxi for the deed, and Óðinn objected that he had given the fine horse to a giantess's son rather than to his own father. The hone stayed in Thor's head. The völva Gróa, wife of Aurvandill the Bold, came to sing it loose with her spells, and the stone was already working free — until Thor, to please her, told how he had carried Aurvandill in a basket out of Jötunheimr, and how the man's frozen toe, broken off and thrown into the sky, became the star called Aurvandill's Toe. Gróa rejoiced so greatly at the news that she forgot her spells; the hone stirs in Thor's head to this day. Therefore, Snorri warns, whetstones must never be thrown across the floor.

myths.title: The Skaldic Witness
myths.text: Snorri quotes his sources, and for this myth the source is Þjóðólfr of Hvin's Haustlöng — a shield-poem composed in the early tenth century, among the oldest mythological verse we have. Þjóðólfr tells the whole combat in dense dróttkvætt: the 'defier of the gods' who rode to the fight, the earth shaking beneath the giant's host, the whetstone bitten from the hard stone of the heart, the hammer answering. That a skald within living memory of the Viking Age's pagan courts could assume his hearers knew the whetstone, the clay giant, and the fall proves the story was not Snorri's construction: it was already old, already fixed, already the standard account of the hardest fight Thor ever fought.

lore.syncretism: Hrungnir resists the usual syncretic moves. Attempts to read him as a reflex of an Indo-European dragon-slaying have been made — a stone-bodied chaos-being struck down by the thunderer's missile does resemble the Vedic Vṛtra pattern — but the fit is partial, since Hrungnir steals nothing, hoards nothing, and threatens no waters; scholars treat the combat as a native Norse contest-epic rather than an inherited myth. His truer company is within the corpus itself: he is one of the named great fights of Þórr, standing between Geirrøðr, killed by a thrown glowing iron, and Hymir, fished with and nearly killed by the sea. The whetstone lodged in Thor's head has been compared with the embedded weapons of other mythologies — the fragment that will not come out — but no source identifies a borrowing, and the handbooks register Hrungnir as a distinctively Norse invention, a giant built of the very landscape the North knew: stone, clay, and weather.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hrungnir's afterlife runs through the skalds before it runs through anyone else: Haustlöng made his fall one of the foundation-texts of Norse poetics, and Snorri cites the poem as the authority for the myth, so that every handbook of Old Norse literature meets him early. The Victorians took up the clay giant — Mǫkkurkálfi recurs in retellings as the archetype of the hollow colossus, all size and mare's heart — and the detail that whetstones must not be thrown across the floor survived in folklore collections as a curiosity of thunder-lore. In modern reception he is the template for every stone-hearted boss the genre has built since: fantasy games and novels cast his duel whenever a hero must fight a mountain that can throw back. His name never entered living use the way Baldr's or Thor's did; it remains exactly what the Edda made it — the name of the strongest thing the hammer ever had to kill.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hrungnir is the Edda's essay on confidence without flexibility. Every part of him is the hardest available material — heart of stone, head of stone, shield of stone — and the myth's arithmetic is that hardness is not the same as strength. The whetstone is the perfect weapon for him: a stone whose entire purpose is to sharpen other things, hurled once, shattering on the first iron it meets. Against him the Edda sets two counter-images. Mǫkkurkálfi, the engineered champion, enormous and empty, a mare's heart quaking in nine leagues of clay — the warning about size without courage. And Magni, three nights old, lifting what all the gods together could not — the warning about measuring strength by age, rank, or expectation. Hrungnir wagered his head on a horse race and lost it in a duel. The name survives, etymology unknown, as the corpus's permanent reminder that being the strongest thing in the room is a wager too — and someone always holds the hammer.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Hrungnir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᚱᚢᚴᚾᛁᛦ (h-r-u-k-n-i-R, the ᚴ-rune writing g and ᛦ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: hrungnir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Hrungnir is a textual figure: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and no picture stone can be securely tied to the duel — though the tradition of carving mythic combat on picture and rune stones is exactly the world his skald belonged to. His material witness is instead a poem about an object: Þjóðólfr of Hvin's Haustlöng was composed for a painted shield, a Viking-Age prestige object bearing mythic scenes, and the verses Snorri quotes are our evidence that the Hrungnir combat belonged to that visual repertoire in the early tenth century. The myth's own materiality is geological: Snorri anchors the shattered whetstone in the landscape — the hone-rocks of the world are its debris — and the taboo against throwing whetstones across the floor entered Scandinavian folk custom as the myth's trace in daily practice. The literary witnesses hang by the usual threads: Skáldskaparmál in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister manuscripts, and the Haustlöng stanzas preserved nowhere else but in Snorri's quotation.
